name: Illusory superiority
statement: On most desirable traits and skills, more people place themselves above the average person than the arithmetic allows.
meaning: The claim is about a distribution rather than about any one rating. Being above average is not an error, because somebody has to be. What the studies find is that the share of people claiming the position is larger than the share that can hold it, so the aggregate is wrong in cases where no individual rating can be shown to be. Svenson put the point in its sharpest form by asking for a position in a percentile ranking, where more than half of a group cannot sit above the median. The effect is defined across traits and skills rather than in one domain, and its size moves with which trait is asked about and how the question is worded.

origin.note: Svenson set out to replicate older claims, which he called poorly documented, that 70 to 80% of drivers put themselves in the safer half. He does not use the label "better-than-average effect" anywhere in the paper.

evidence: Svenson gave written questions to 161 licensed drivers. Eighty-one answered an advertisement in a University of Oregon student paper, median age 22, and 80 were psychology students at the University of Stockholm, median age 33. Each person judged either skill or safety, not both, by marking one of ten successive 10% intervals. The comparison group was the other people in the room, named in the question and set explicitly against Eugene, Oregon or against Sweden. On skill, 93% of the American sample and 69% of the Swedish put themselves above the median driver, and 46.3% of the Americans claimed the most skilful fifth. On safety the figures were 88% and 77%. The paper reports no statistical test. Zell, Strickhouser, Sedikides and Alicke later pooled 291 independent samples from 124 published articles and more than 950,000 participants, and put the effect at dz = 0.78, 95% CI [0.71, 0.84], with little evidence of publication bias.

replication.headline: A preregistered replication with 1,203 American drivers found the effect on all three response scales it tried.
replication.detail: Koppel, Andersson, Tinghög, Västfjäll and Feldman ran the study online in 2019, moving the comparison group from people in the room to drivers in the participant's US state. On Svenson's own percentile scale, 94% placed themselves above the median driver for safety, 95% CI [0.91, 0.96], and 91% did so for skill, [0.88, 0.94]. A seven-point Likert version gave Hedges's g = 1.39 for safety and g = 1.19 for skill, the figure in the field below. The third scale is the informative one. Adding an explicit 50% midpoint to the percentile categories left safety at 91% and dropped skill to 78%, because 14.6% of participants took the midpoint rather than a side. Effect sizes on the three scales had overlapping intervals, so the authors call the finding stable across them. What the midpoint moved was the share above the median, not the effect size.

study.cite: Koppel, L., Andersson, D., Tinghög, G., Västfjäll, D., & Feldman, G. (2023). We are all less risky and more skillful than our fellow drivers: Successful replication and extension of Svenson (1981). Meta-Psychology, 7, MP.2021.2932.

limits: The comparison target does most of the work, and it need not be the self. Klar and Giladi ran eight studies in which participants judged an anonymous student, individuated in one version by nothing but an ID number, as better than the average student and above the group median. A ninth reversed it: an anonymous member of a disliked out-group was rated worse than that group's average. Their reading is that people have difficulty comparing a singular target with a generalised one, and enriching the description of the average student reduced the effect. Giladi and Klar then found the same superiority and inferiority pattern in judgments of objects and concepts across six experiments, which they take as support for a cognitive account over a social one. Chambers and Windschitl argue in a review that ordinary information-processing limits can produce above-average effects with no motive to self-enhance. The effect also reverses. Kruger reported a below-average effect in domains where absolute skill tends to be low, and cognitive load made both directions worse, which fits people anchoring on their own ability and adjusting too little for everyone else's. Korbmacher, Kwan and Feldman replicated that with 756 participants. Ratings came out above average on all four easy domains and below average on three of the four difficult ones. The correlation between domain difficulty and comparative rating was r = -0.85, 95% CI [-0.97, -0.37]. Zell and colleagues found the pooled effect larger for personality traits than for abilities, and larger in studies using the direct method than the indirect one. One number in the replication does not agree with itself: the text gives 93% for safety on the reproduced scale where the table gives 0.94, from 386 of 413 participants either way.
misreadings: Svenson's figure travels badly. It is quoted as 93% of drivers rating themselves above average, when it was 41 American students rating driving skill against the other people in the room; the matching Swedish figure was 69%, and the safety figures were 88% and 77%. Above average and above the median are also different claims, and only the second is capped at half a group. This is not the Dunning-Kruger effect, which asks whether poor performers in particular misjudge themselves. Illusory superiority is a statement about the whole distribution and predicts nothing about who is worst. It is not on its own evidence of self-flattery either, since Klar and Giladi's anonymous student was rated above average by people with no stake in him.
